Actually f at the endpoints is zero, interior negative, so the interior critical point will be a minimum (global min in that interval). Similarly for (r3,r4). So each negative interval has exactly one interior critical point that is a local minimum (since f is negative inside and zero at endpoints). Could there be more than one critical point inside the interval? Possibly if f' has more zeros within that interval. But given the shape of f, it's likely only one. However, given f' is rational with at most three positive zeros overall, and we have two negative intervals each requiring at least one zero, that accounts for two zeros. The third zero (if any) would be in the positive region (maybe between r2 and r3?). Actually f' could have a root in the positive interval (r2,r3) corresponding to a local maximum (since f > 0 there). That would be the third critical point. So typical shape: f' has three positive zeros: one in each interval (r1,r2) (min), (r2,r3) (max), (r3,r4) (min). This matches earlier speculation.

Thus for any ordering of the roots (distinct), there will be exactly three critical points: minima in each negative interval and a maximum in the positive interval between the two positive intervals (i.e., between r2 and r3). So indeed f' will have three simple positive zeros for generic k (distinct). So global minima are the two minima in negative intervals.

Now the values of f at these minima will generally be different. The problem asks for values of k such that those minima are equal.

Thus the problem reduces to solving for k such that the minima in intervals (r1,r2) and (r3,r4) have equal f value.

Thus we need to find k such that the local minima in left negative interval and right negative interval have the same value.

Now we need to find these minima as functions of k.
